lesson.title: Mania: When Energy and Judgment Come Apart
lesson.summary: Mania is a distinct period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood and greatly increased energy that impairs functioning, distinguishing it from the milder, less disruptive state of hypomania.
lesson.body:
A manic episode is defined as a distinct period, lasting at least a week (or any length if hospitalization is required), of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood, present most of the day, nearly every day, along with a marked increase in energy or goal directed activity. That mood and energy shift has to be accompanied by at least three additional symptoms from a specific list (or four, if the prevailing mood is irritable rather than elevated): inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, unusually talkative or pressured speech, racing thoughts or a rapid flow of ideas, distractibility, a marked increase in goal directed activity or physical restlessness, and excessive involvement in risky activities such as impulsive spending, reckless driving, or poor investment decisions. For the episode to count as full mania rather than hypomania, it must cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning, require hospitalization to prevent harm, or include psychotic features like delusions.

What makes mania dangerous is exactly the combination of symptoms that can look, from the outside, like enviable qualities: boundless energy, sky high confidence, minimal need for sleep, a flood of ideas. Inside a manic episode, though, judgment deteriorates along with everything else. Grandiosity can convince someone they are capable of things they are not. Decreased need for sleep is not the same as feeling well rested, it reflects a genuine disruption of the body's regulatory systems. Impulsivity paired with inflated confidence is a common recipe for real world harm: emptying a bank account on a spending spree, making major decisions with no ability to weigh consequences, or taking physical risks without appropriate caution. This is why mania, unlike an ordinary burst of enthusiasm or a productive week, is treated as a psychiatric emergency in its more severe forms, since the person's ability to protect their own safety and interests can be genuinely compromised.

The distinction between mania and hypomania is really a distinction of severity and consequence rather than of the underlying symptom list. Hypomania involves many of the same features, elevated mood, increased energy, decreased sleep, but for a shorter minimum duration of four days, without the marked functional impairment, without hospitalization, and without psychosis. A useful way to hold the two together: hypomania is noticeable, mania is disruptive. Since a full manic episode is the single defining requirement for bipolar I disorder, mania is not a symptom that happens to appear alongside that diagnosis, it is the criterion that creates it.
